blocks.html: 2. What a condition variable is
blocks.text: 2. What a condition variable is

blocks.html: A condition variable is a synchronization primitive that lets threads wait efficiently for a condition to become true.
blocks.text: A condition variable is a synchronization primitive that lets threads wait efficiently for a condition to become true.

blocks.html: Here is a catch, the thread which actually waits, sleeps. And it does not have to observe the conditional variable or anything. When the condition becomes true, OS very likely will have to wake it up. One more catch, OS is like the boss, it can wake the thread up, even when its not required.
blocks.text: Here is a catch, the thread which actually waits, sleeps. And it does not have to observe the conditional variable or anything. When the condition becomes true, OS very likely will have to wake it up. One more catch, OS is like the boss, it can wake the thread up, even when its not required.

blocks.html: The thing is, OS will definitely wake up the thread, if things are ready, but if OS wakes up the thread, then it does not mean that things are ready. So, there must be check, that will run on wake up to know if things are ready or not.

blocks.html: 4. Real software engineering example: Thread Pool Job Queue

blocks.html: This is the most common use case you’ll see in production code. Web servers, background workers, image processors — they all use this.
blocks.text: This is the most common use case you’ll see in production code. Web servers, background workers, image processors — they all use this.

blocks.html: The problem: You have 8 worker threads. You have 1000 jobs coming in at random times. You don’t want to spawn 1000 threads. You want the 8 threads to pick up jobs as they arrive, and sleep when there’s no work.
blocks.text:
The problem:
You have 8 worker threads. You have 1000 jobs coming in at random times. You don’t want to spawn 1000 threads. You want the 8 threads to pick up jobs as they arrive, and sleep when there’s no work.

blocks.html: Without condition variables: Each thread polls the queue. Wastes CPU. With condition variables: Threads sleep until a job exists. 0 CPU when idle.
blocks.text:
Without condition variables: Each thread polls the queue. Wastes CPU.
With condition variables: Threads sleep until a job exists. 0 CPU when idle.

blocks.html: Complete C++ example:
blocks.text: Complete C++ example:

blocks.html: #include <mutex> #include <condition_variable> #include <queue> #include <thread> #include <functional> class ThreadPool { private: std::vector<std::thread> workers; std::queue<std::function<void()>> jobs; std::mutex queue_mutex; // Protects the job queue std::condition_variable cv; // The waiting room + bell bool shutdown = false; // The condition we care about public: ThreadPool(size_t num_threads) { for (size_t i = 0; i < num_threads; ++i) { workers.emplace_back([this] { worker_loop(); // Each thread runs this }); } } void submit(std::function<void()> job) { { // Scope for lock_guard std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(queue_mutex); jobs.push(std::move(job)); // 1. Make condition true } // lock released here cv.notify_one(); // 2. Wake one sleeping worker } ~ThreadPool() { { std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(queue_mutex); shutdown = true; // Signal we’re done } cv.notify_all(); // Wake ALL workers so they can exit for (auto& t : workers) t.join(); } private: void worker_loop() { while (true) { std::function<void()> job; { // Critical section std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(queue_mutex); // Wait until: we have a job OR we're shutting down cv.wait(lock, [this] { return!jobs.empty() || shutdown; }); // If shutting down and no jobs left, exit thread if (shutdown && jobs.empty()) return; job = std::move(jobs.front()); jobs.pop(); } // mutex unlocked here job(); // Run the job WITHOUT holding the lock } } }; // Usage: ThreadPool pool(8); // 8 worker threads, all sleeping initially pool.submit([] { process_image("cat.jpg"); }); pool.submit([] { send_email("user@example.com"); }); // Workers wake up instantly, no polling, no wasted CPU
What happens step by step:
blocks.text: What happens step by step:

blocks.html:
Startup: 8 threads call
worker_loop()
. All hit
cv.wait()
immediately because
jobs.empty()
is true. All 8 go to sleep. CPU usage = 0%.
blocks.text: Startup: 8 threads call worker_loop(). All hit cv.wait() immediately because jobs.empty() is true. All 8 go to sleep. CPU usage = 0%.

blocks.html:
Job arrives: Main thread calls
submit()
. It locks, pushes job, unlocks, calls
notify_one()
.
blocks.text: Job arrives: Main thread calls submit(). It locks, pushes job, unlocks, calls notify_one().

blocks.html: OS wakes one worker: The OS picks one sleeping thread from cv’s wait queue and makes it runnable.
blocks.text: OS wakes one worker: The OS picks one sleeping thread from cv’s wait queue and makes it runnable.

blocks.html:
Worker re-checks: Worker wakes up with mutex re-locked. The
while
condition
!jobs.empty() || shutdown
is now true, so it exits
wait()
, pops job, unlocks, runs job.
blocks.text: Worker re-checks: Worker wakes up with mutex re-locked. The while condition !jobs.empty() || shutdown is now true, so it exits wait(), pops job, unlocks, runs job.

blocks.html:
Idle again: After running job, worker loops back, finds queue empty, calls
wait()
again and sleeps.
blocks.text: Idle again: After running job, worker loops back, finds queue empty, calls wait() again and sleeps.

blocks.html:
Why not use a semaphore? You could.
semaphore jobs_available
. But now you have two things to keep in sync: the queue size AND the semaphore count. With cv + mutex, there’s only one source of truth:
jobs.empty()
. If you push and forget to
signal()
, the job just sits there. If you
signal()
and forget to push, workers wake up for nothing. Cv forces you to tie the signal to the actual state change.
blocks.text:
Why not use a semaphore?
You could. semaphore jobs_available. But now you have two things to keep in sync: the queue size AND the semaphore count. With cv + mutex, there’s only one source of truth: jobs.empty(). If you push and forget to signal(), the job just sits there. If you signal() and forget to push, workers wake up for nothing. Cv forces you to tie the signal to the actual state change.

blocks.html: Rule of thumb: If you already have a mutex protecting data, and you need to wait for some property of that data to change, use a condition variable. If you just need to count permits, use a semaphore.

Condition variables don’t store the condition. You store
bool ready
. The cv only handles sleeping/waking.

Always

The mutex protects the condition. You must hold it to check the condition and to call

You sleep for free. 10,000 waiting threads use ~0 CPU until
notify()
is called.
